Chapter One: The Pursuit of Power Over Shared Security.
Picture this—you’re sitting around a kitchen table with a few close friends, sharing stories and worries as the world outside feels like it’s spinning faster every day.
Someone, the history buff of the group, leans in and wonders, “Why do some countries act like the whole world is theirs to control?”
Before you know it, the conversation lands on the United States—a country that’s shaped global events in more ways than most of us realize.
And it leads to a big question: What really happens when a single nation decides its own interests matter more than everyone else’s?
Let’s take a closer look at how the U.S. has chased global dominance.
After World War Two, the world was in shambles. The United States stood almost alone, with unmatched economic and military power.
The temptation to use that power to shape the future? It was huge.
But instead of joining others to create a safer, more cooperative world, the U.S. often chose to go it alone—setting its own rules and expecting everyone to follow.
Over the years, this became a habit. When a crisis hit—be it Latin America, the Middle East, or Southeast Asia—American leaders started viewing the world like a chessboard, shifting pieces to protect their own interests.
They used words like “democracy” and “freedom” to justify these moves.
But on the ground, things were rarely that simple. Real people, in faraway places, ended up caught between their own struggles and the ambitions of a distant superpower.
Here’s a story that really brings it home.
Imagine a small town in Central America, where families are just trying to rebuild after years of conflict. They dream of peace, but instead, they’re forced to live in fear. Outside forces come in, arming and training local militias—all under the banner of fighting communism.
Suddenly, their daily lives are shaped by decisions made thousands of miles away, in rooms filled with maps and strategies. The promise of democracy? It doesn’t mean much when it shows up at the end of a rifle.
And back in the U.S., most folks never see this side of the story. The news is full of official statements and patriotic images, but rarely the human cost.
That gap—the one between the language of freedom and the reality of violence—just keeps growing with each new conflict.
It becomes clear that chasing dominance isn’t just about security. It’s about holding onto power—no questions asked.
But here’s something to pay attention to: Acting alone, the U.S. often undermined international agreements and organizations that were supposed to keep the peace.
The United Nations, which was meant to give every nation a voice, got pushed aside whenever it clashed with American interests.
International law? It was used when convenient, ignored when it wasn’t.
And these choices didn’t just affect distant countries.
At home, the focus on military strength and overseas threats shaped what people cared about—and what the government spent money on.
Resources that could’ve gone to things like education, health care, or fighting poverty were instead funneled into weapons and foreign operations.
The idea that safety only comes through dominance became a self-fulfilling prophecy—making everyone, in the end, a bit less safe.
As the friends around that kitchen table wrap up their talk, one of them asks, “Isn’t there a better way? Couldn’t we choose cooperation over control, shared security over going it alone?”
The question lingers, hanging in the air, as the world keeps trying to make sense of the choices made in the name of power.
